solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Product of confused dreaming, but real — a once-in-a-lifetime destination?

indicators.note: confused tells us the letters of the next words are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone's dream holiday spot, half-imagined and half-real, visited only once in a lifetime.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a dark joke: a place you go once because ships and planes are said to vanish there and never return.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says vessels entering this stretch of the Atlantic disappear, so a trip there is one you would make only once.

clue.text: Born support musician

parts.note: b is the abbreviation for born, as in genealogies
to assist is to support or help

explanation.surface: Someone born to be a backing musician in a band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'support' suggests a support act, but here it gives ASSIST.
explanation.definitionFit: A bassist plays the bass guitar or double bass, one kind of musician.

clue.text: Early 19th century vehicle's identified by this concise encyclopedia

parts.note: a reg, short for registration, is the number plate identifying a vehicle
ency is the short form of encyclopedia

explanation.surface: An old reference book claims to identify vintage vehicles from the early 1800s.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a car's 'reg' is its registration number, shown on its plates.
explanation.definitionFit: The British Regency ran from 1811 to 1820, and the name covers the style of that early 19th-century era.

clue.text: World body cut corners dreadfully, one from 1950s having failed to move with the times

definitions.text: having failed to move with the times

parts.note: the UN, United Nations, is the world body

indicators.note: dreadfully says the letters are treated badly, mangled into a new order

parts.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter
a Ted, or Teddy boy, was a 1950s youth in Edwardian-style clothes

explanation.surface: An international body skimped dreadfully, like some relic of the fifties who never moved on.
explanation.walkthrough: Teddy boys were a 1950s British youth subculture; 'dreadfully' rearranges CUTCORNERS into RECONSTRUC.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unreconstructed holds old-fashioned views and has not adapted to modern attitudes.

clue.text: A kind of loving? The opposite

definitions.note: a noun for the reverse of loving, that is dislike; loving here is read as a noun

parts.note: a version is a kind or variant of something

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about a type of love, answered that it is quite the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A kind of' reads as one phrase, but 'of' only links A VERSION to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An aversion is a strong dislike, the opposite of a fondness or love for something.

clue.text: Leaders of the group in defeat in low spirits?

indicators.note: in places the leading letters inside the word for defeat

parts.note: a rout is a heavy defeat

indicators.note: the leaders of words are their first letters

explanation.surface: The group's leaders feel depressed after a defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'low spirits' looks like gloom, but means poor-quality alcohol.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotgut is cheap, rough liquor, so spirits of low quality, as the question mark hints.

clue.text: Might bowler be let go so peremptorily?

definitions.text: Might bowler be let go so peremptorily?

parts.words: Might bowler be let go so peremptorily?
parts.note: a bowler is a hat, and letting it go is dropping it; a sacked cricket bowler pictured as dropped without warning

explanation.surface: A cricket team sacks its bowler abruptly without any warning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bowler' looks like a cricketer being dropped, but is the hat; the idiom means instantly, without hesitation.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means at once and with no hesitation, from a hat dropped as a starting signal.

clue.text: Forcing out unionist government outwardly making progress

indicators.note: outwardly means the progress word is on the outside, wrapping the other letters

parts.note: going, as in getting going, means making progress
U is the abbreviation for Unionist, as in Northern Irish politics

explanation.surface: A Unionist government is pushed out of office despite appearing to make progress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forcing out' can mean ousting from office, but here it is scooping out, as with an eye.
explanation.definitionFit: To gouge is to dig or force something out, as with a chisel or a thumb.

clue.text: Former lover allowed pictures to be made public

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
a person who posed sat still and allowed photos to be taken

explanation.surface: Someone's ex agreed to private photos being published.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one sentence, but splits at 'be': POSED is 'allowed pictures to be', then 'made public'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something exposed has been revealed or laid open to everyone, a synonym for made public.

clue.text: Plant used to sweeten retro tomato sauces — mash soundly

indicators.note: retro means looking backwards, so the word for the sauces is read from its end

parts.note: ragus are Italian meat sauces cooked with tomato

indicators.note: soundly says the word is to be judged by how it is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: to mash something is to beat it

explanation.surface: A cook's recipe tip: sweeten an old-fashioned tomato sauce, then mash it thoroughly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soundly' looks like 'thoroughly' but signals a word heard: BEAT sounds the same as BEET.
explanation.definitionFit: This root crop is grown and refined to make table sugar, so it is a plant whose use is sweetening.

clue.text: Trade Union member picketing hospital for strike

indicators.note: pickets stand around a workplace, so the union letters surround the hospital letter

parts.note: H is the map and sign abbreviation for hospital
MP, Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A union official on a picket line outside a hospital during a strike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strike' sits naturally with the picket line, but it is the definition in the sense of a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: To thump someone is to hit them hard, a synonym for strike as a verb.

clue.text: Superhuman — bowled out in classic style

indicators.note: out says a letter is thrown out of the word for superhuman

parts.note: bionic, like the Bionic Man, means with superhuman powers
b is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for bowled

explanation.surface: A superhero is bowled out in a cricket match played in the classic manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bowled out' looks like one cricket phrase; 'bowled' gives B and 'out' removes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ionic order is one of the classical styles of Greek architecture, with scroll-shaped capitals.

clue.text: See if wandering past backward places makes confused

indicators.note: past means beyond, so the shuffled letters come after the reversed word
backward tells us to read the word for places in reverse

parts.note: to place something is to put it, so places gives puts

indicators.note: wandering letters stray from their order, signalling an anagram

explanation.surface: Someone told to look as they wander past places that seem to go backwards, leaving them bewildered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' turns PUTS into STUP, and 'wandering' rearranges SEEIF into EFIES.
explanation.definitionFit: To stupefy is to stun or bewilder someone, so it is a synonym for makes confused.

clue.text: Seeing fit to prosecute charity in case of intoxication

parts.note: to try someone is to prosecute them in court

indicators.note: in places the charity letters inside the outer pair
the case of a word is its outside, its first and last letters

parts.note: an NGO, non-governmental organisation, is typically a charity

explanation.surface: Deciding whether to take a drunk-driving case to court, or whether a charity should be prosecuted.
explanation.walkthrough: The case of 'intoxication' is I and N, and NGO goes between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting on clothes in a shop to check whether they fit is seeing if they fit, a playful reading of the phrase.

clue.text: Beginning to freeze stiff?

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: rigid means stiff, unbending

explanation.surface: Someone out in the cold, feeling themselves start to freeze solid.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: something icy cold and stiff.
explanation.definitionFit: Frigid means intensely cold, as when one is starting to freeze solid.

clue.text: Show off cereal bowl

parts.note: bran is a breakfast cereal made from husks of grain
a dish is a bowl

explanation.surface: A proud person displays a breakfast bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show off' reads as a boast but is a verb meaning wave about.
explanation.definitionFit: To brandish something is to wave it about to display it, so to show it off.

clue.text: England, following on, are in for payback

indicators.note: following puts the England letter after the others

parts.note: re means on or about, as in a memo heading
in cricket a side that is in is batting, so are in gives bat

explanation.surface: A cricket report: England, made to follow on, go in to bat seeking revenge.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a side forced to 'follow on' must bat again at once; here 'on' and 'are in' are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebate is money paid back to a customer, a refund, so payback in the financial sense.

clue.text: Sweet bachelor breaking into a dance

indicators.note: breaking into says the bachelor letter forces its way inside the other letters

parts.note: the rumba is a Cuban ballroom dance
B is the abbreviation for bachelor, as in degrees like BA

explanation.surface: A single man cuts in on a dance; a sweet romantic moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' looks like an adjective for the scene but is a noun, a dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A rum baba is a small yeast cake soaked in rum syrup, served as a dessert.

clue.text: Boredom's chronic in place for retired people

indicators.note: chronic, in its slang sense of dreadful, signals the letters are mangled

parts.note: the word boredom, with 's as is linking to the indicator

explanation.surface: A lament that boredom is endemic in a retirement home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired people' suggests pensioners, but means people who have gone to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To retire can mean going to bed for the night, and a bedroom is where people sleep.

clue.text: Cooks skins beforehand?

parts.note: pre is the prefix meaning before or beforehand
to pare fruit is to skin or peel it

explanation.surface: A chef peels vegetables before the cooking starts.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks that the answer, read as PRE-PARES, is skins beforehand.
explanation.definitionFit: To prepare a meal is to cook it, so the two verbs are synonyms in the kitchen.

clue.text: Following recipe, added trimmed meat to pan with head of endive and stirred again

indicators.note: following puts the other pieces after the recipe letter

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for recipe, from Latin recipe on prescriptions

indicators.note: trimmed cuts away the ends, keeping the middle

parts.note: a wok is a Chinese frying pan

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Cooking instructions: add trimmed meat to the pan with endive and stir again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stirred again' looks like more kitchen work but means woke up once more.
explanation.definitionFit: To stir is to wake or rouse, so having reawoken is to have stirred from sleep again.

clue.text: Harsh noise from church covered by 'rock', loosely

indicators.note: in a down entry, covered by means the church letters sit underneath

parts.note: scree is loose broken rock on a mountain slope

explanation.surface: A grating sound from a church buried beneath a rockfall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loosely' looks like an anagram signal, but it is part of the definition of SCREE.
explanation.definitionFit: A screech is a loud, shrill cry, a kind of harsh noise.

clue.text: Only two elements, to be precise

parts.note: just means only, as in just one
S is the symbol for sulphur and O the symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A chemist insists, precisely, that there are only two elements.
explanation.definitionFit: Just so means exactly or precisely, in a neat and correct manner.

clue.text: Turning dusky gold, Tuesday's moon not full at time of harvest?

indicators.note: turning round the word for dusky reverses it

parts.note: dim means dusky, poorly lit
Au is the chemical symbol for gold
Tu is the short form of Tuesday

indicators.note: a moon that is not full is hollowed out here, keeping only its outside letters

explanation.surface: A golden harvest moon rising on a dusky Tuesday evening, just short of full.
explanation.walkthrough: The harvest moon is the full moon nearest the September equinox; here 'not full' empties MOON to MN.
explanation.definitionFit: Harvest is gathered in September and October, the middle of autumn; the question mark allows the loose fit.

clue.text: Intuitive ability held back by mateRIAL Facts

indicators.note: held back says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Instinct is restrained by the hard facts of the case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held' hints at containment and 'back' at reversal: the letters sit inside 'material facts' and read right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: Flair is a natural talent or instinctive aptitude, a synonym for intuitive ability.

clue.text: Could it be a legend happening?

parts.note: split as leg end, the foot is the end of a leg

explanation.surface: A puzzled question whether some tale might be a legend come true.
explanation.walkthrough: 'legend' must be read as LEG END, which is the FOOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something afoot is under way or going on, a synonym for happening.

clue.text: One supporting hip kind of school gets second-highest mark in style

indicators.note: in places the school word and grade inside the word for style

parts.note: tone means style or character, as in the tone of a place
a high school is a kind of secondary school
B is the grade below A

explanation.surface: A pupil at a high school, propped up by a friend, earns a B for flair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hip' looks like the slang for stylish, chiming with 'style', but it is the joint the bone meets.
explanation.definitionFit: The femur runs from knee to hip and bears the body's weight, so it supports the hip joint.

clue.text: Prepared for battle, using choppers to transport weapons?

definitions.meaning: fully equipped with arms, ready to fight
choppers is slang for teeth, so this pictures a pirate with a knife clamped in their teeth

explanation.surface: A military operation flies in arms by helicopter ahead of a battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'choppers' looks like helicopters but is slang for teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone carrying as many weapons as possible, fully ready for a fight.
